key_insight: In the 2024–2025 U.S. flu season, influenza vaccine effectiveness estimates were broadly similar between prospective test-negative enrollment and electronic health record (EHR) data.
clinical_relevance: This suggests EHR-based surveillance can potentially complement traditional prospective studies for seasonal influenza vaccine effectiveness monitoring, while still requiring attention to subgroup differences.
method: Prospectively enrolled outpatients with acute respiratory symptoms and tested respiratory specimens for influenza.
Built a parallel EHR cohort of medically attended acute respiratory illness encounters with linked diagnosis, testing, and vaccination data.
Estimated vaccine effectiveness in both sources using adjusted logistic regression comparing vaccination among influenza-positive versus influenza-negative patients.
evidence_signal: Across 6,793 prospectively enrolled patients and 282,444 EHR MAARI encounters, effectiveness was 36% and 38%, respectively, with similar confidence intervals overall.
watch_item: Findings were less consistent in adults aged 65 years and older, where the prospective estimate was imprecise and diverged from the EHR-based estimate.
paper_title: Comparison of Influenza Vaccine Effectiveness Estimates Using Test-Negative Prospective Enrollment and Electronic Health Record Data, United States, 2024--2025
